mainEntity.name: How much does a Mercedes-Benz A-Class 180d engine replacement cost in the UK?

acceptedAnswer.text: A replacement engine for an A180d typically costs between £600 and £5,000 depending on the engine code and condition. Used OM607 units start from £600-£1,500, reconditioned from £1,800-£3,200, and fully rebuilt OM654 engines from £2,800-£5,000. Labour for supply & fit adds £400-£800.

mainEntity.name: Does the Mercedes-Benz A-Class 180d have a timing belt or timing chain?

acceptedAnswer.text: It depends on the engine. The OM607 (W176 facelift, 2014-2018) and OM608 (W177, 2018-2020) are Renault-sourced 1.5-litre engines with a timing belt that must be replaced every 80,000-100,000 miles. The OM654 (W177, 2020-present) is Mercedes' own 2.0-litre engine with a timing chain. Enter your registration above to confirm which engine is fitted to your car.

mainEntity.name: Is it worth replacing the engine in a Mercedes-Benz A-Class 180d?

acceptedAnswer.text: It depends on the generation and condition. A W176 A180d is typically worth £4,000-£10,000 - a rebuilt OM607 engine (£2,200-£3,800) can be a worthwhile investment if the car is in good condition. A W177 A180d is worth £8,000-£18,000 - a rebuilt OM654 engine (£2,800-£5,000) is usually well within the car's value.

mainEntity.name: How long does a Mercedes-Benz A-Class 180d engine last?

acceptedAnswer.text: The OM607 and OM608 (Renault-sourced 1.5-litre) are capable of high mileage, but their timing belts must be replaced every 80,000-100,000 miles - failure to do so is catastrophic. The OM654 (Mercedes 2.0-litre) is more robust and can exceed 200,000+ miles with proper maintenance. Regular oil changes (every 10,000 miles) and timely replacement of wear items are key to maximising engine life.

mainEntity.name: What is the difference between the OM607, OM608 and OM654 engines in the A180d?

acceptedAnswer.text: The OM607 is a 1.5-litre Renault K9K-sourced diesel used in the W176 A180d facelift (2014-2018), producing 109 hp with a timing belt. The OM608 is an updated 1.5-litre version used in the early W177 A180d (2018-2020), producing 116 hp (+7 hp) with the same timing belt architecture. The OM654 is Mercedes' own 2.0-litre diesel introduced in late 2020, producing 116 hp but with a timing chain and 20 Nm more torque.

mainEntity.name: What causes the Mercedes-Benz A-Class 180d AdBlue system to fail?

acceptedAnswer.text: The AdBlue system on A180d models (all engines) can fail due to crystallisation in the dosing injector, a failed heater element in the AdBlue tank, or degraded NOx sensors. The ECU responds with a 'No Start in XXX miles' countdown when AdBlue dosing is compromised. These faults are common on 2016-2019 models and can be expensive to repair at main dealers.

historyTimeline.h2: Mercedes-Benz A-Class 180d - Engine History & Specs at a Glance
historyTimeline.intro: The A180d badge replaced the "180 CDI" naming with the W176 facelift in 2014, using a Renault-sourced 1.5-litre OM607 diesel. The W177 generation launched in 2018 with an updated OM608 version of the same engine, before switching to Mercedes' own 2.0-litre OM654 in late 2020 - a significant shift from belt-driven Renault architecture to chain-driven Mercedes engineering.

milestones.description: OM607 DE 15 (607.951), 1.5L diesel, 109 hp - W176 A180d facelift launch; Renault K9K-sourced engine with timing belt
OM608 DE 15, 1.5L diesel, 116 hp - W177 A180d launch; updated Renault-sourced engine, +7 hp over OM607
OM654 DE 20 (654.920), 2.0L diesel, 116 hp - W177 A180d switches to Mercedes' own engine; timing chain replaces belt; +20 Nm torque

commonProblems.h3: The A180d has been powered by three different diesel engines across its production life - the Renault-sourced OM607 (W176 facelift), the updated OM608 (early W177), and Mercedes' own OM654 (late W177). Each has distinct failure patterns. Rebuilt A180d engines through EnginesMarket include upgraded components addressing the original failure points, plus a minimum 12-month unlimited-mileage warranty.

problems.h4: OM607 / OM608 Timing Belt Failure - The Renault-Sourced Engine's Critical Weak Point
problems.affectedModels: Mercedes-Benz A-Class 180d (OM607.951 and OM608, W176 facelift and early W177, 2014-2020)
problems.rootCause: The OM607 and OM608 are Renault K9K-sourced engines that use a timing belt rather than a chain. The belt must be replaced every 80,000-100,000 miles - failure causes piston-to-valve contact and complete engine destruction.

repairOptions.whatItInvolves: Replace timing belt, tensioner, water pump
repairOptions.longevity: Essential maintenance; do not exceed 100k miles

repairOptions.whatItInvolves: Supply & fit rebuilt engine with new belt and tensioner
repairOptions.longevity: Required if belt has snapped; valves and pistons damaged

problems.vehicleValueCheck: A typical W176 A180d is worth £4,000-£10,000, while a W177 A180d is worth £8,000-£18,000 depending on condition and mileage. For OM607/OM608 vehicles, a preventative belt replacement (£350-£650) is significantly cheaper than a full engine replacement (£2,200-£4,000). For vehicles approaching 80,000 miles, the belt change is a non-negotiable maintenance item.
problems.recommendation: Unlike chain-driven engines, the OM607 and OM608's timing belt failure is predictable and preventable. If your A180d is approaching 80,000 miles or 5 years since the last belt change, replace it immediately. A £350-£650 specialist belt change is far cheaper than a £2,200+ engine replacement.
problems.cta: -> Compare OM607 / OM608 timing belt replacement and engine prices for your A-Class 180d

problems.group: OM607 / OM608 / OM654 AdBlue System Failure
problems.h4: OM607 / OM608 / OM654 AdBlue System Failure - "No Start in XXX Miles" Warnings
problems.affectedModels: Mercedes-Benz A-Class 180d (OM607.951, OM608 and OM654.920, W176 and W177, 2014-present)
problems.rootCause: The AdBlue (SCR) system components - heater elements, dosing injectors, and NOx sensors - are prone to failure. The ECU responds with a "No Start in XXX miles" countdown when AdBlue dosing is compromised.

repairOptions.tier: AdBlue Tank Heater or Injector Replacement
repairOptions.whatItInvolves: Replace failed heater element or dosing injector, clear fault codes, perform SCR reset
repairOptions.longevity: Requires specialist diagnostic tools to identify the exact component

repairOptions.whatItInvolves: Replace upstream and/or downstream NOx sensors, ECU software reset
repairOptions.longevity: Common on 2016-2019 models; sensors have a limited service life

repairOptions.whatItInvolves: Complete engine with updated emissions components and injectors
repairOptions.longevity: Only if engine has been run with repeated SCR failures causing EGR clogging

problems.recommendation: When the countdown appears, don't ignore it. A mobile AdBlue specialist can often diagnose and repair heater or injector faults for half the dealer cost. For vehicles over 100,000 miles facing repeated SCR issues, compare the cost of repairs against replacement.
problems.cta: -> Get quotes for OM607, OM608 and OM654 engine replacement for your A180d

problems.group: OM607 / OM608 Injector Seal & Turbocharger Issues
problems.h4: OM607 / OM608 Injector Seal & Turbocharger Issues
problems.affectedModels: Mercedes-Benz A-Class 180d (OM607.951 and OM608, W176 facelift and early W177, 2014-2020)
problems.rootCause: Injector seal failure is common on both OM607 and OM608, causing combustion gas blow-by and poor cold starting. Turbo actuator failure is also reported on higher-mileage units.

repairOptions.whatItInvolves: Remove injectors, replace seals and bolts
repairOptions.longevity: Viable if injectors are not seized

repairOptions.whatItInvolves: Replace turbo actuator or complete turbocharger
repairOptions.longevity: For boost issues; catch early to avoid turbo failure

repairOptions.whatItInvolves: Complete engine with new injectors and turbo components
repairOptions.longevity: Required if injectors are seized or turbo has failed catastrophically

problems.recommendation: If you experience poor cold starting or a chuffing noise from the engine bay, have the injector seals inspected. Replacing all four seals at a specialist costs £350-£600 and is far cheaper than the £1,800+ bill for injector replacement if they seize.
